metadata.title: Gebser v. Lago Vista Independent School Dist., 524 U.S. 274 (1998) (No. 96-1866)
metadata.creator: Supreme Court of the United States
metadata.description:
Case name: Gebser v. Lago Vista Independent School Dist.

Opinion filed: 1998-06-22

Docket No.: 96-1866

Citations:
• 141 L. Ed. 2d 277
• 118 S. Ct. 1989
• 524 U.S. 274
• 1998 U.S. LEXIS 4173

Case holding summaries:
• a Title IX case drawing an analogy to the deliberate indifference standard of 1983
• adopting a “deliberate indifference” standard as being in line with the promise of the statute’s administrative enforcement scheme of an official decision by the federal funds recipient not to remedy the violation
• “[I]t would “frustrate the purposes” of Title IX to permit a damages recovery against a school district for a teacher’s sexual harassment of a student based on principles of respondeat superior or constructive notice, i.e., without actual notice to a school district official.”
• equating deliberate indifference to "an official decision not to remedy the violation"
• explaining that Title IX liability is predicated upon notice to an "appropriate person" and an opportunity to remedy any violation
• requiring proof of actual notice and deliberate indifference before a school district is liable under Title IX for a teacher’s sexual harassment of a student
• private right of action for damages under Title IX encompasses intentional sex discrimination in the form of a recipient’s deliberate indifference to teacher’s sexual harassment of a student
• describing the development of the implied private right of action
• "The two statutes [Title VI and Title IX] operate in the same manner, conditioning an offer of federal funding on a promise by the recipient not to discriminate, in what amounts essentially to a contract between the Government and the recipient of funds." (emphasis added)
• applying the "deliberate indifference" standard in the context of Title IX
• school district cannot be held liable for harassment of student by teacher based on principles of constructive notice or vicarious liability under Title IX.
• noting that “[w]hen Congress at taches conditions to the award of federal funds under its spending power . . . private actions holding the recipient liable in monetary damages” are permissible
• requiring that a student who is sexually harassed by a teacher prove both actual notice to and deliberate indifference by a school district for such an entity to be held liable for damages under Title IX
• requiring proof of actual notice and deliberate indifference before a school district is liable under Title IX for a teacher’s sexual harassment of a student
• stating that the complaint did not state a valid claim under the Title IX because notice of inappropriate comments by a teacher during class was "plainly insufficient to alert the principal to the possibility that [the teacher] was involved in a sexual relationship with a student"
• describing administrative enforcement provisions of Title IX, which are nearly identical to those of Title VI, and stating that “the regulations do not appear to 3508 COLWELL v. HHS contemplate a condition ordering payment of monetary dam- ages”
• finding that courts have "a measure of latitude" to determine "when it is appropriate to award monetary damages" for violations of Title IX of the Education Amendments of 1972
• equating deliberate indifference to “an official decision 14 Although one could argue that this approach was not wise, that is not the question before us. 17 not to remedy the violation”
• finding that complaints regarding whether a teacher made inappropriate comments during class did not alert the principal to the possibility that such a teacher was involved in a sexual relationship with one of his students
• plaintiff may not recover against school district for alleged Title IX violations by employee based solely on principles of respondeat superior
• plaintiff may not recover against school district for alleged Title IX violations by employee based solely on principles of respondeat superior
• "Because Congress did not expressly create a private right of action under Title IX, the statutory text does not shed light on the scope of available remedies."
• describing administrative enforcement provisions of Title IX, which are nearly identical to those of Title VI, and stating that "the regulations do not appear to contemplate a condition ordering payment of monetary damages"
• rejecting the application of vicarious liability and agency principles as grounds for triggering liability under Title IX
• finding notice to the school district indispensable before it can be held financially liable under Title IX for a teacher's sexual harassment of a student, but not requiring active approval of such harassment
• holding that Title IX's implied private right of action will not lie in absence of school district's "deliberate indifference" to teacher's conduct upon actual receipt of notice thereof
• holding that a teacher’s sexual harassment of a student constitutes discrimination under Title IX
• information insufficient to alert principal to possibility of teacher's sexual relationship with student
• "We attempt to infer how the ... Congress [at the time of enactment] would have addressed the issue."
• "[W]e generally examine the relevant statute to ensure that we do not fashion the scope of an implied right in a manner at odds with the statutory structure and purpose."
• explaining that actual knowledge by an “appropriate person”—someone who “has authority to address the alleged discrimination and to institute corrective measures”—is required
• We must "`attempt to infer'" from all available indicia "`how the [1972] Congress would have addressed the issue had the ... action been included as an express provision in the' statute."
• plaintiff may not recover against school district for alleged Title IX violations by employee based solely on principles of respondeat superior
• stat- ing that courts implying rights of action “have a measure of latitude to shape a sensible remedial scheme that best comports” with the relevant enactment
• plaintiff may not recover against school district for alleged Title IX violations by employee based solely on principles of respondeat superior
• discussing monetary damages under Title IX
• concluding failure to comply with a regulation “does not itself constitute ‘discrimination’ under Title IX”
• requiring “actual knowledge of discrimination in the recipient‟s programs and fail[ure] [to] adequately . . . respond”
• finding a school not vicariously liable for sexual harassment by a teacher of a student, when the school did not have notice of the harassment
• a Title IX case drawing an analogy to the deliberate indifference standard of § 1983
• finding a school not vicariously liable for sexual harassment by a teacher of a student, when the school did not have notice of the harassment
• finding that “a complaint from parents of other students charging only that [the teacher] had made inappropriate comments during class . . . was plainly insufficient to alert the principal to the possibility that [the teacher] was involved in a sexual relationship with a student”
• no respondeat superior claims for Title IX claims of employee-student harassment
• stat- ing that courts implying rights of action “have a measure of latitude to shape a sensible remedial scheme that best comports” with the relevant enactment
• holding school was not vicariously liable under Title IX for teacher’s sexual harassment of student when school had no notice of harassment
• "Title IX focuses 11 more on `protecting' individuals from discriminatory practices carried out by recipients of federal funds."
• permitting administrative enforcement of regulation requiring college to execute an "Assurance of Compliance" with Title IX
• "`A disregard of the command of the statute is a wrongful act, and where it results in damage to one of the class for whose especial benefit the statute was enacted, the right to recover the damages from the party in default is implied, according to a doctrine of the common law' "
• "When the school board accepted federal funds, it agreed not to discriminate on the basis of sex. We think it unlikely that it further agreed to suffer liability whenever its employees discriminate on the basis of sex"
• "We have no doubt that Congress intended to create Title IX remedies comparable to those available under Title VI and that it understood Title VI as authorizing an implied private cause of action for victims of the prohibited discrimination"
